summary: Defines a simple application-layer protocol that lets remote users inspect or change management information on a gateway. It was an interim answer to immediate gateway monitoring needs. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1028 defines a simple way for a remote computer to inspect or change the settings of a router. The idea is that everything about a router that a manager might want to know or alter is a named variable, so the router only has to support reading a variable and writing a variable. The variables travel as messages encoded in the CCITT X.409 format, inside an authentication session carried over UDP.

subtitle: An early way to read and change the settings of an Internet router from a remote machine.

tldr.problem: Gateways needed to be monitored, and the monitoring had to be built into the gateway itself. Every new management command added to the gateway meant more software to write, test and get right.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol models all gateway management as reading or writing named parameter values, so the gateway implements only two operations. The variables are named by octet strings, hold only integers or octet strings, and are exchanged as four message types written in the CCITT X.409 encoding, carried over UDP inside an authentication session.

sections.title: An Interim Answer to Gateway Monitoring
sections.content:
The memo is distributed to members of the Internet community in order to solicit reactions to the proposals it contains. It says that while the issues discussed may not be directly relevant to the research problems of the Internet, they may be interesting to a number of researchers and implementors.

It defines a simple application-layer protocol by which management information for a gateway may be inspected or altered by logically remote users. The proposal is intended only as an interim response to immediate gateway monitoring needs while work on more elaborate and robust designs proceeds with the care and deliberation appropriate to that task. Accordingly, long term use of the mechanisms described in the memo should be seriously questioned as more comprehensive proposals emerge in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors are explicit that this is a stopgap. Gateways needed monitoring straight away, and a full management design was going to take time, so this memo offers something small enough to build now and says plainly that it should not be relied on for long.

sections.title: The Design Decisions
sections.content:
The protocol is shaped by the desire to minimise the number and complexity of management functions the gateway itself realises. The memo argues this in four ways: the development cost of gateway software is reduced; the amount of management function that can be supported remotely is increased, admitting the fullest use of Internet resources in the management task and imposing the fewest possible restrictions on the form and sophistication of management tools; and a simplified set of management functions is easily understood and used by developers of gateway management tools. A second goal is that the paradigm for monitoring and control be sufficiently extensible to accommodate additional, possibly unanticipated aspects of gateway operation. A third goal is that the design be, as much as possible, independent of the architecture and mechanisms of particular hosts or particular gateways.

Eight decisions follow from those goals. First, all gateway management functions are modelled as alterations or inspections of parameter values, so that a protocol entity on a logically remote host interacts with a protocol entity resident on the gateway to alter or retrieve named portions of the gateway state. This limits the essential management functions on the gateway to two, one to assign a value to a configuration parameter and one to retrieve such a value, and it avoids support for imperative management commands, whose number grows and whose semantics are arbitrarily complex. An imperative command can still be accommodated, by making it the setting of a parameter value that subsequently triggers the desired action.

Second, any needed authentication functionality is realised in a distinct protocol layer that provides services to the monitoring protocol itself, which reduces the complexity of the individual layers and eases implementation. Third, the identity of an application protocol entity is known to its peers only by the services of the underlying authentication protocol, which implies a model of access control where access to gateway variables is managed in terms of the association between application entities and authentication sessions. Multi-level access is then supported by multiple instances of the application protocol entity, each characterised by the set of gateway variables it knows, the mode of access, READ-ONLY or READ-WRITE, afforded to that set, and the authentication protocol session it belongs to.

Fourth, the conventions of the CCITT X.409 recommendation are adopted for representing the information exchanged between protocol entities. The cost is a modest increase in implementation complexity; the benefit is that protocol data are represented on the network in a machine-independent, widely understood and widely accepted form, and that the form of the messages can be concisely described in the X.409 language.

Fifth, the variables manipulated by the protocol assume only integer or octet string type values. Sixth, the exchange of protocol messages requires only an unreliable datagram transport, and every protocol message is entirely and independently representable by a single transport datagram. The memo specifies the exchange via UDP but notes that the design is in general suitable for a wide variety of transport mechanisms. Seventh, the variables are named by octet string values. This departs from the architectural traditions of the Internet, where objects are identified by assigned integer values, but the octet string name space can manifest flat or hierarchical structure, so a single simple mechanism can provide both random access to individual variables and sequential access to semantically related groups, and the name space can be extended to accommodate unforeseen needs without compromising the relationships among existing variables. Eighth, the number of unsolicited messages is minimised, so that the monitoring of network state is accomplished primarily by polling from the monitoring centre, and the definition of unsolicited messages is confined to those strictly necessary to guide the monitoring centre about the timing and focus of its polling.
sections.plainLanguage: The central decision is that nothing about a router is controlled by a command. A command would need new code in the router every time one was invented, and its behaviour would have to be defined. Instead everything is a setting with a name and a value, and the router only ever reads or writes settings. The other decisions follow from that: authentication is kept in its own layer so the monitoring code stays small, values are only numbers or strings, names are strings so they can be grouped and extended, and the router almost never sends anything unasked for, because the monitoring centre does the asking.

sections.title: The Four Message Types
sections.content:
Communication among application protocol entities is by the exchange of protocol messages using the services of the authentication protocol, and each such message is entirely and independently represented by a single message of that protocol. An implementation need not accept protocol messages whose length exceeds 484 octets. The type of a protocol message is indicated by the value of the implicit type tag for the data structure it represents, according to the conventions of CCITT X.409.

Four message types are recognised. The Get Request carries a request identifier, an error status, an error index and a list of variable operations, each of which pairs a variable name with a value. On receipt, if the name in some variable operation does not lexicographically precede the name of some variable known to the receiving entity, the reply is a Get Response with the error status set to gmp_err_nix_name and the error index set to the unit-based index of that component. If the Get Response would exceed the largest message the protocol definition requires to be accepted, the reply carries gmp_err_too_big and an error index of zero. Otherwise the reply is a Get Response whose components give the name and value of the variable that immediately succeeds the requested name in the lexicographic ordering of all variable names known to the receiving entity, with the error status gmp_err_noerror and the error index zero, and the same request identifier as the request. Get Request messages are generated only at the request of the application user.

The Get Response has the same form as the Get Request, differing only in the indication of message type, and the response of a protocol entity to it is to present its contents to the application user. Get Response messages are generated only upon receipt of Set Request or Get Request messages.

The Trap Request carries a trap type and a list of values whose significance is implementation-specific. Interpretations for negative trap types are implementation-specific, while five non-negative values are defined: 0, the cold start trap, means the sending entity is reinitialising itself in a way that may alter the gateway configuration or the protocol entity implementation; 1, the warm start trap, means it is reinitialising itself in a way that alters neither; 2, the link failure trap, means it recognises a failure in one of the communication links represented in the gateway configuration; 3, the authentication failure trap, means it is the addressee of a protocol message that is not properly authenticated; and 4, the EGP neighbour loss trap, means an EGP neighbour for whom it was a peer has been marked down and the peer relationship no longer obtains.

The Set Request has the same form as the Get Request, differing only in the message type. On receipt, if the name in some variable operation names no variable known to the receiving entity, the reply is a Get Response with the error status gmp_err_nix_name and the error index of that component. If the contents of the value field do not, according to CCITT X.409, manifest a type, length and value consistent with that required for the named variable, the reply carries gmp_err_bad_value and the error index of that component. If the response would exceed the largest message the protocol requires to be accepted, the reply carries gmp_err_too_big and an error index of zero. Otherwise each value is assigned to the variable named in the matching component, in the order the components appear, and the reply is a Get Response with gmp_err_noerror and an error index of zero. Recognition and processing of Set Request messages is not required by the protocol definition.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of message: ask for a variable, the answer to that ask, a change to a variable, and an unsolicited notice from the router. Errors are reported in the reply itself, with a status code and the position in the request that caused it. The router is allowed to ignore change requests altogether, since the memo says the protocol does not require them.

sections.title: The Authentication Protocol
sections.content:
The authentication protocol is a session-layer protocol by which messages specified by a protocol user are selectively delivered to other protocol users. The protocol definition precludes delivery to a protocol user of any user message for which the protocol representation lacks a specified authentic form. Communication among authentication protocol entities is accomplished by the exchange of protocol messages, each of which is entirely and independently represented by a single UDP datagram. An authentication protocol entity responds to protocol messages received at UDP port 153 on the host with which it is associated.

A half-session of the authentication protocol is, for any ordered pair of protocol users, the set of messages sent from the first user of the pair to the second. A session is the union of two complementary half-sessions, the set of messages exchanged between a given pair of protocol users. Each half-session is associated with a triplet of functions. The authentication function for a half-session is a boolean-valued function that characterises the set of authentication protocol messages that are of acceptable, authentic form. The message interpretation function maps the messages accepted by the authentication function to the set of all possible user messages. The message representation function is the inverse of the message interpretation function. The association between half-sessions and triplets of functions is not defined in the memo.

One message type is recognised, the Data Request, made up of four fields. The Message Length field gives the length of the message as an unsigned 16-bit binary integer, encoded so that more significant bits precede less significant bits in the order of transmission, and it includes the length of the Message Length field itself. The Session ID Length field gives the length in octets of the Session ID field, as an unsigned 8-bit binary integer. The Session ID field names the protocol session to which the message belongs, encoded as a sequence of octets of that length. The User Data field carries the message being passed from one protocol user to another, encoded according to the conventions implicit in the message representation function for the appropriate half of the session named by the Session ID field.

On receipt, the receiving authentication protocol entity verifies the form of the message by applying the authentication function associated with its half of the named session. If the form is accepted as authentic, the user message computed by applying the message interpretation function is presented to the protocol user together with an indication of the session it belongs to. Otherwise the message is discarded and an indication of the receipt of an unauthenticated message is presented to the protocol user.
sections.plainLanguage: Every monitoring message is wrapped in an authentication session, which is a separate layer that decides whether a message is genuine before passing it on. Each session has a name, and each direction of a session has its own rule for what a valid message looks like and how to interpret it. The wrapper travels as one UDP datagram to port 153 on the host.

sections.title: Variable Names and Required Variables
sections.content:
The variables retrieved or manipulated by the application protocol are named by octet string values. A name may be represented numerically as a sequence of hexadecimal numbers, each denoting the value of the corresponding octet, or symbolically as a character string whose form reflects the sequence of octets while suggesting the semantics of the named variable. The symbolic form of the name of zero length is the character string of zero length, and the symbolic form of a name of non-zero length n is the concatenation of the symbolic form of the name formed by the first n-1 octets with the underscore character and a string that does not include the underscore, so that the result is unique among the symbolic representations for all names of length n.

So the names 01 01 01, 01 01 02, 01 02 01, 01 03 01 03 01, 01 03 01 03 02, 01 03 01 04 01 and 01 03 01 04 02 might be represented symbolically as _GW_version_id, _GW_version_rev, _GW_cfg_nnets, _GW_net_if_type_net1, _GW_net_if_type_net2, _GW_net_if_speed_net1 and _GW_net_if_speed_net2. All variable names are terminated by an implementation specific octet string of non-zero length, so a complete variable name is not specified for any of the variables defined in the memo; for each defined variable some prefix portion of its name is specified, with the understanding that the rightmost portion is specific to the protocol implementation.

Fullest exploitation of the semantics of the Get Request message requires that names for related variables be chosen so as to be contiguous in the lexicographic ordering of all variable names, so that one request can walk through a group of them. An implementation may present variables in addition to those defined in the memo, provided no implementation-specific variable is presented as having the name of one defined here. By convention the names of implementation-specific variables share a common prefix that distinguishes them from those defined in the memo and from those of other implementations; the memo gives the example of variables specific to version 1.3 of the Squeaky gateway product of the Swinging Gateway company, named 01 FF 01 01 13 01, 01 FF 01 01 13 02 and 01 FF 01 01 13 03. Names beginning 02, symbolically _HOST, and names beginning 03, symbolically _TS, are reserved for future use.

Where the information represented by a variable defined in the memo is also represented internally by a gateway, access to that variable must be afforded by at least one application protocol entity associated with the gateway. The required variables are _GW_version_id, an octet string value identifying the protocol entity implementation; _GW_version_rev, an integer identifying the revision level of that implementation; and _GW_cfg_nnets, an integer giving the number of logical network interfaces afforded by the configuration of the gateway. Each network interface is uniquely identified by an octet string, and the convention for naming them is implementation-specific. For each interface there are classes of variable: _GW_net_if_type, an integer giving the type of the interface, _GW_net_if_speed, an integer giving the estimated nominal bandwidth in bits per second, _GW_net_if_in_pkts and _GW_net_if_out_pkts counting packets received and transmitted, _GW_net_if_in_bytes and _GW_net_if_out_bytes counting octets received and transmitted, _GW_net_if_in_errors and _GW_net_if_out_errors counting reception and transmission errors, and _GW_net_if_status, an integer giving the current status of the interface.

The memo also defines variables for the Internet Protocol interfaces of the gateway, for the Exterior Gateway Protocol, including a variable for the EGP neighbour state, and for routing information, and it adds interface-specific classes for Ethernet and for the serial lines of the Proteon p4200 Internet Router gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Variable names are strings rather than numbers, and the strings are written so that related names sit next to each other in alphabetical order. That means one request can walk through a whole group of related settings, such as the packet counters for one interface, by asking for each name in turn. Each name is a prefix plus a part the implementation chooses, so vendors can add their own settings without colliding with the standard ones.

items.title: Variables, not commands
items.text: The gateway only reads and writes named values.

items.title: Identity from the authentication layer
items.text: Access rights follow the authenticated session.

items.title: Integers and octet strings only
items.text: Two value types, so little to implement.

items.title: Unreliable datagram transport
items.text: Each message fits in one datagram; no resending.

items.title: Octet string variable names
items.text: Names can be grouped and extended without renumbering.

items.title: Few unsolicited messages
items.text: The monitoring centre polls; the router mostly stays quiet.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MESSAGE TYPES AND THEIR X.409 TAGS

items.label: Get Request
items.desc: Asks for the values of one or more variables, or for the variable that follows a given name.

items.label: Get Response
items.desc: The answer to a Get Request or a Set Request, carrying the error status and the values.

items.label: Trap Request
items.desc: An unsolicited notice from the gateway, such as a cold start or a link failure.

items.label: Set Request
items.desc: Asks the gateway to change the value of a variable. Processing these is not required.
